Learning funcml with NeuroVigil: Interpretable and Equitable Prediction of MCI-to-Alzheimer's Conversion

This tutorial is a hands-on learning resource for students. It follows one real project, NeuroVigil, from raw data to a deployed application, and uses it to teach the funcml workflow: resampling, learner comparison, tuning, fitting, interpretation and calibration, followed by the steps a clinical model needs on top of that (decision thresholds, decision curves, a fairness audit and a robustness check). Every code block is taken from the project scripts and every output is the one those scripts print.

AuthorAya Lahlifi
CM6RI, AI Department
SupervisorImad El Badisy
Frameworkfuncml
Code and appGitHub and live app
Launch the live app GitHub repository funcml tutorial

Abstract

A model that discriminates well is not automatically ready for the clinic: it may be poorly calibrated, opaque, or less accurate for some patient groups. This tutorial shows, step by step, how to build and validate a model that predicts conversion from Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) to Alzheimer's disease (AD) within 24 months on the ADNI cohort with the funcml framework, assessing five properties jointly: discrimination, calibration, interpretability, clinical utility and fairness. The pipeline is leakage-safe (split before KNN imputation, imputation fitted on predictors only, thresholds chosen on a validation set, test set used for final evaluation only), stratifies patients with two thresholds (a Youden screening threshold and a specificity-oriented "Rule-In" threshold targeting 90% specificity on validation), and combines permutation importance, accumulated local effects and SHAP. On 1,288 MCI patients, a tuned XGBoost model reaches a held-out test AUC of 0.871 (95% CI 0.824 to 0.919) and an expected calibration error of 0.056. The tutorial reports its limitations openly, including right-censored labels, small subgroups, an APOE-ε4 disparity (ΔAUC = 0.087) and the absence of external validation. The final model is deployed as NeuroVigil, a trilingual (French, English, Arabic) R Shiny application.

Keywords

R package, funcml, Alzheimer's disease, mild cognitive impairment, XGBoost, interpretability, calibration, decision curve analysis, algorithmic fairness, ADNI, tutorial

1 Introduction

Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) is a prodromal stage of Alzheimer's disease from which roughly 10 to 15% of patients convert each year (Petersen 2004). Predicting conversion within a clinically actionable window (24 months) can guide follow-up, trial enrolment and care planning. Gradient-boosted trees discriminate well on this task, but discrimination (AUC) is only one of several properties a model needs before it can be trusted at the bedside. Real clinical data contain missing values that naive handling can bias; tree ensembles are opaque to the clinicians who must act on them; and performance that looks strong overall can hide degradation in specific subgroups.

This tutorial follows one project from raw data to a deployed application and shows where each of five properties is checked (Table 1), in the spirit of the TRIPOD reporting guideline for prediction models (Collins et al. 2015). It uses funcml (El Badisy 2026), the formula-first framework built around six verbs: fit(), evaluate(), tune(), compare_learners(), interpret() and estimate(). The project uses fit(), tune(), compare_learners() and interpret(), together with the resampling constructor cv().

Note: preprocessing outside funcml

funcml expects preprocessing (imputation, encoding, scaling) to happen before any funcml call, so that the data passed to fit() is exactly the data being modelled. In this project the preprocessing is done with recipes, and the saved recipe is reused to impute new patients in the app.

2 Installation and Data

2.1 Installation and project layout

remotes::install_github("ielbadisy/funcml")
install.packages(c("here", "tidyverse", "recipes", "pROC", "xgboost", "ranger", "gbm"))
# for the app: shiny, DT, readxl, writexl, base64enc

Open NeuroVigil.Rproj in RStudio and run every script from a clean R session.1 No script contains an absolute path. Each one starts with source(here::here("R", "00_config.R")), which finds the project root with the here package and defines the paths and constants shared by all scripts:

DATA_ROOT <- Sys.getenv("NEUROVIGIL_DATA", unset = here::here("data"))
PATHS <- list(raw       = file.path(DATA_ROOT, "raw", "FINAL_DATASET.csv"),
              processed = file.path(DATA_ROOT, "processed"),
              outputs   = here::here("outputs"))

SEED            <- 42
HORIZON_MONTHS  <- 24
MAX_MISSING_PCT <- 60
TEST_FRACTION   <- 0.20
VAL_FRACTION    <- 0.20
ID_COLS         <- c("RID", "event", "time_to_event", "target")    # never used as predictors
DROP_COLS       <- c("EXAMDATE", "STATUS", "subject_id", "entry_date", "visit")
NON_PREDICTORS  <- c(ID_COLS, "GENOTYPE", "a_une_irm")             # excluded from the model formula

Place FINAL_DATASET.csv in data/raw/, or keep the ADNI data outside the repository and point to them with Sys.setenv(NEUROVIGIL_DATA = "path/to/data") (the folder must contain raw/FINAL_DATASET.csv). Generated data go to data/processed/ and tables and figures to outputs/. Because every constant lives in one file, changing the horizon or the seed means editing one line, and all scripts stay consistent.

2.2 The ADNI cohort and the target

FINAL_DATASET.csv has one row per MCI patient (1,288 patients, 72 columns, from ADNI-1, ADNI-2 and ADNI-GO; Petersen et al. 2010; access is granted on application at adni.loni.usc.edu) with event and time_to_event. The target is conversion within HORIZON_MONTHS = 24 months:

df_brut <- df_brut %>%
  mutate(target = factor(if_else(event == 1 & time_to_event <= HORIZON_MONTHS, "Yes", "No"),
                         levels = c("No", "Yes")))
print(table(df_brut$target))
#>   No  Yes
#> 1047  241

The cohort has 241 converters (18.7%). Predictors span demographics, cognitive scores (MMSE, MoCA, CDR-SB, FAQ, ADAS-Cog), APOE genotype, CSF biomarkers (Aβ42, tau, p-tau), plasma lipids and proteomic markers, and FreeSurfer MRI morphometry.

Patients who did not convert but were followed for less than 24 months are also labelled No: 350 of the 1,047 "No" patients (33%), 208 of them followed for less than 12 months. Their true 24-month status is unknown, which adds label noise to every metric computed below.2

2.3 Running the whole pipeline

scripts/run_all.R runs the five scripts in order. Start from a clean session:

for (s in c("01_data_preparation.R", "02_train_model.R", "03_temporal_robustness.R",
            "04_prediction_nouveau_patient.R", "05_dca_fairness.R")) {
  message("==== ", s, " ====")
  source(here::here("scripts", s), echo = FALSE)
}

3 The NeuroVigil Workflow

Figure 1 shows the deployed system. A clinician enters data manually or uploads an Excel/CSV file; the server recodes the inputs, imputes the missing values with the recipe saved by script 01, runs the XGBoost model saved by script 02 and assigns one of three risk levels with the thresholds saved in the metrics file. The result comes back with recommendations and a downloadable PDF report. Everything the server needs is produced by scripts 01 to 04.

Note: design principle

The test set is used for final evaluation only. It never takes part in fitting the imputation, in model selection or in threshold selection. After the model is fixed, it is used to compute interpretation plots, calibration, decision curves and the fairness audit.

4 Data Preparation (01_data_preparation.R)

4.1 Variable selection and recoding

Columns with more than 60% missing values are dropped (11 of the 72), together with identifiers and dates. Among the retained columns, missingness ranges from 0.08% (MMSE) to 57.6% (MoCA and the proteomic markers). GENOTYPE (for example "3/4") is converted to n_e4, the number of ε4 alleles.

keep   <- names(which(colMeans(is.na(df_brut)) <= MAX_MISSING_PCT / 100))
df_sel <- df_brut %>%
  select(all_of(keep), -any_of(DROP_COLS)) %>%
  mutate(PTGENDER = factor(PTGENDER, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("Homme", "Femme")),
         n_e4     = str_count(GENOTYPE, "4"),            # number of APOE-e4 alleles
         GENOTYPE = factor(GENOTYPE))
cat("Columns kept:", ncol(df_sel), "\n")
#> Columns kept: 58

The 58 columns are the 4 outcome and identifier columns (RID, event, time_to_event, target), GENOTYPE, and 53 predictors. Counting columns like this is a cheap check that the selection did what you intended.

4.2 Split before imputation, then KNN imputation

The split comes first, and the imputation is fitted on the training set only. Missing values are filled by k-nearest-neighbour imputation (Troyanskaya et al. 2001) with the recipes package (Kuhn, Wickham, and Hvitfeldt 2024). The recipe sees predictors only: the outcome columns are kept aside and re-attached afterwards. If event or time_to_event entered the recipe, for example through recipe(target ~ ., data = train_raw), the imputed values would carry outcome information into both sets, a classic form of data leakage (Kaufman et al. 2012) that Section 11 quantifies.

set.seed(SEED)
idx_test  <- sample(nrow(df_sel), size = round(TEST_FRACTION * nrow(df_sel)))
train_raw <- df_sel[-idx_test, ]
test_raw  <- df_sel[idx_test, ]

vars_imp    <- setdiff(names(train_raw), ID_COLS)
recipe_prep <- recipe(~ ., data = train_raw[vars_imp]) %>%
  step_impute_knn(all_predictors(), neighbors = 5) %>%
  prep(training = train_raw[vars_imp])

data_train <- bind_cols(train_raw[ID_COLS], bake(recipe_prep, new_data = train_raw[vars_imp]))
data_test  <- bind_cols(test_raw[ID_COLS],  bake(recipe_prep, new_data = test_raw[vars_imp]))

stopifnot(!anyNA(data_train), !anyNA(data_test),
          length(intersect(data_train$RID, data_test$RID)) == 0)
saveRDS(recipe_prep,  proc_path(FILES$recipe))      # reused by the app (contains ADNI training data: do not commit)
#> TRAIN: 1030 | TEST: 258
#> Converters  TRAIN: 188 | TEST: 53

The stopifnot() line turns three silent assumptions into checks: no value is left missing, and no patient appears in both sets. The converter rate is 18.3% in training and 20.5% in test.

5 Modeling (02_train_model.R)

The training data are split once more: 824 patients to fit and tune, and 206 held out to choose the decision thresholds. One resampling object is created and reused, so that every learner and every configuration is scored on the same five folds.

vars_predicteurs <- setdiff(names(data_train_full), NON_PREDICTORS)
formula_cls      <- reformulate(vars_predicteurs, response = "target")

set.seed(SEED)
idx_val  <- sample(nrow(data_train_full), size = round(VAL_FRACTION * nrow(data_train_full)))
data_val <- data_train_full[idx_val, ]
data_fit <- data_train_full[-idx_val, ]

resampling_cv <- cv(v = 5, seed = SEED)
#> Fit: 824 | Validation: 206 | Test: 258
funcml: reformulate() builds the formula from a character vector, which avoids typing 53 names. funcml is formula-first: the formula is the single statement of what is modelled (funcml tutorial §3).

5.1 Baseline benchmark

Five learners are compared under the same 5-fold cross-validation on AUC, log-loss and accuracy, with default hyperparameters. This is Step 1 of the funcml end-to-end workflow.

cmp_cls <- compare_learners(
  data = data_fit, formula = formula_cls,
  models = c("glm", "rpart", "ranger", "gbm", "xgboost"),
  resampling = resampling_cv, metrics = c("accuracy", "auc", "logloss"),
  type = "prob", seed = SEED)
print(cmp_cls); plot(cmp_cls)
#> <funcml_compare> task: classification | tuned: FALSE
#>      model   metric      mean          sd n   std_error conf_level  conf_low conf_high tuned rank

#> 5    rpart      auc 0.7156005 0.055045485 5 0.024617089       0.95 0.6472525 0.7839485 FALSE    5
#> 6    rpart  logloss 0.7850587 0.432140023 5 0.193258894       0.95 0.2484860 1.3216314 FALSE    5

Note: why XGBoost?

In this untuned benchmark, ranger has the highest AUC and accuracy and the lowest log-loss, gbm is close behind, and XGBoost ranks fourth on AUC. The confidence intervals overlap, so no learner is clearly best. XGBoost is retained for its compatibility with the SHAP, PDP and ALE tools of interpret(), not for superior performance, and it is not compared with tuned ranger or gbm models. Its high default log-loss (0.580) is a sign of over-confident probabilities with default settings, which tuning (smaller learning rate, shallower trees) addresses.

Try it

Add "glmnet" to models and rerun the benchmark: a regularised GLM is a stronger baseline than glm with 53 correlated predictors. Then score XGBoost alone with evaluate(data = data_fit, formula = formula_cls, model = "xgboost", resampling = resampling_cv, metrics = c("auc", "logloss"), type = "prob", seed = SEED) (funcml tutorial §7).

5.2 Tuning

Random search over 8 of the 12 configurations of the grid, with AUC as the criterion (Step 2 of the funcml workflow). The full results are written to outputs/hyperparameter_grid.csv.

grid_xgb <- expand.grid(nrounds = c(100, 200), max_depth = c(3, 4, 6), eta = c(0.05, 0.1))
tuned <- tune(data = data_fit, formula = formula_cls, model = "xgboost",
              grid = grid_xgb, resampling = resampling_cv, metric = "auc",
              search = "random", n_evals = 8, type = "prob", seed = SEED)
print(tuned$best)
write.csv(as.data.frame(tuned$results), out_path("hyperparameter_grid.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
#>   nrounds max_depth  eta      mean         sd n  std_error conf_level conf_low conf_high
#> 1     100         3 0.05 0.8242542 0.03013149 5 0.01347521       0.95 0.786841 0.8616674

Try it: nested cross-validation

The CV AUC of the selected configuration is slightly optimistic, because the same folds served to choose it. Add outer_resampling = cv(v = 5, seed = 1) to the tune() call to estimate the performance of the whole tuning procedure (funcml tutorial §8.3).

5.3 Final model

fit_final <- fit(formula = formula_cls, data = data_fit, model = "xgboost",
                 spec = as.list(tuned$best[1, ]))
print(fit_final)
#> <funcml_fit> classification model: xgboost
#> Formula: target ~ PTGENDER + entry_age + PTEDUCAT + CDGLOBAL + CDRSB + [...] + n_e4
#> Features: 53 | Obs: 824

tuned$best[1, ] also contains the summary columns (mean, sd, ...); only the hyperparameter columns are used by the XGBoost learner. The model is fitted on the 824 fit patients only: the validation set stays untouched until the thresholds are chosen.

6 Decision Thresholds

6.1 Theory

Rather than fixing τ = 0.5, two thresholds are derived on the validation set. The lower (screening) threshold maximises Youden's index (Youden 1950; Fluss, Faraggi, and Reiser 2005):

J(τ) = Sensitivity(τ) + Specificity(τ) − 1, τlow = arg maxτ J(τ)

The upper ("Rule-In") threshold maximises J among the thresholds whose validation specificity is at least 90%. The 90% target is a validation-set target, not a guarantee of test-set or future performance:

τhigh = arg maxτ : Spec(τ) ≥ 0.90 J(τ)

Patients are then classified as Low (p < τlow), Moderate (τlow ≤ p < τhigh) or High risk (p ≥ τhigh).

6.2 R code

probs_val  <- predict(fit_final, data_val, type = "prob")[, "Yes"]
labels_val <- data_val$target

seuils_test <- seq(0.01, 0.99, by = 0.001)
metrics_df  <- data.frame(
  seuil = seuils_test,
  sens  = sapply(seuils_test, function(s) mean(probs_val[labels_val == "Yes"] >= s)),
  spec  = sapply(seuils_test, function(s) mean(probs_val[labels_val == "No"]  <  s)))
metrics_df$youden <- metrics_df$sens + metrics_df$spec - 1

seuil_bas <- metrics_df$seuil[which.max(metrics_df$youden)]                 # Youden optimum

spec_cible <- 0.90
candidats  <- metrics_df %>% filter(spec >= spec_cible)
if (nrow(candidats) == 0) stop("No threshold reaches the target specificity on the validation set.")
seuil_haut <- candidats$seuil[which.max(candidats$youden)]                  # Rule-In
stopifnot(seuil_haut > seuil_bas)
#> Low threshold  (Youden)  : 0.124 | sens 0.892 | spec 0.716
#> High threshold (Rule-In) : 0.369 | sens 0.405 | spec 0.905
#> Low 60.7% | Moderate 24.3% | High 15.0% (validation)

The validation set has 37 converters and 169 non-converters. A sensitivity of 0.892 means 33 of the 37 converters are above τlow; at τhigh, 15 of 37 are. The three levels contain 125, 50 and 31 of the 206 validation patients.

With only 37 validation converters, a specificity of at least 90% at τhigh holds by construction on the validation set; Section 7.3 shows how both thresholds behave on the test set.

7 Final Evaluation on the Test Set

7.1 Discrimination

Script 02 computes the test AUC directly from ranks. The AUC is the probability that a randomly chosen converter receives a higher score than a randomly chosen non-converter, which is the Mann–Whitney statistic divided by the number of converter/non-converter pairs:3

probs_test  <- predict(fit_final, data_test, type = "prob")[, "Yes"]
labels_test <- data_test$target
pos <- probs_test[labels_test == "Yes"]; neg <- probs_test[labels_test == "No"]
r   <- rank(c(pos, neg))
auc_test <- (sum(r[seq_along(pos)]) - length(pos) * (length(pos) + 1) / 2) / (length(pos) * length(neg))

The script does not print a confidence interval; it can be added in the same session with pROC (Robin et al. 2011), calling it with pROC:: because pROC and funcml both export a function named auc:

roc_test <- pROC::roc(labels_test, probs_test, levels = c("No", "Yes"), direction = "<")
pROC::ci.auc(roc_test, method = "delong")      # 0.824 to 0.919 around 0.871

The test AUC is 0.871 (95% CI 0.824 to 0.919, DeLong), against a cross-validated 0.824 (95% CI 0.787 to 0.862). With 258 test patients (53 converters) the test estimate is imprecise, as its interval shows; the gap between the two figures is compatible with sampling variability and should not be read as the model doing better on new patients.

7.2 Calibration

The expected calibration error (ECE) is the bin-size-weighted mean absolute gap between the mean predicted probability and the observed event rate over M equal-frequency bins Bm (Naeini, Cooper, and Hauskrecht 2015; funcml tutorial §6.4). Calibration matters as much as discrimination when a probability is shown to a clinician (Van Calster et al. 2019):

ECE = Σm=1..M (|Bm| / n) · | acc(Bm) − conf(Bm) |
cal_final <- interpret(fit_final, data_test, method = "calibration",
                       type = "prob", pos_level = "Yes", bins = 10)
plot(cal_final, style = "curve")

ece_tbl <- tibble(prob = probs_test, label = as.integer(labels_test == "Yes")) %>%
  mutate(tranche = ntile(prob, 10)) %>% group_by(tranche) %>%
  summarise(gap = abs(mean(prob) - mean(label)) * n(), n = n())
ece_test <- sum(ece_tbl$gap) / sum(ece_tbl$n)
cat(sprintf("TEST AUC = %.3f | ECE = %.3f\n", auc_test, ece_test))
#> TEST AUC = 0.871 | ECE = 0.056

We report ECE = 0.056 throughout.4 With about 26 patients per bin, both the ECE and the curve are imprecise, and the curve under-estimates risk in the mid-range bins (about 0.43 predicted versus 0.58 observed). Calibration is therefore acceptable, not excellent.

7.3 Performance at both thresholds

The test-set performance at each threshold is obtained with a short loop run after script 02, in the same session:

for (s in c(seuil_bas, seuil_haut)) {
  pred <- probs_test >= s
  cat(sprintf("tau=%.3f  sens=%.3f  spec=%.3f  PPV=%.3f\n", s,
      mean(pred[labels_test == "Yes"]), mean(!pred[labels_test == "No"]),
      mean(labels_test[pred] == "Yes")))
}
#> tau=0.124  sens=0.887  spec=0.683  PPV=0.420
#> tau=0.369  sens=0.604  spec=0.893  PPV=0.593

Table 5: Performance at the two thresholds, on the validation set (selection) and on the test set.

ThresholdValueSensitivitySpecificityPPVSet
Low (Youden)0.1240.8920.716n/avalidation (n = 206)
Low (Youden)0.1240.8870.6830.420test (n = 258)

On the test set the screening threshold behaves as designed (sensitivity 0.887, 47 of 53 converters). At the Rule-In threshold, test specificity is 0.893, close to but below the 90% target: 54 patients are flagged High risk, of whom 32 are converters (PPV 0.593), against a prevalence of 20.5%.

8 Interpretation

8.1 Global importance: permutation

Permutation importance (Fisher, Rudin, and Dominici 2019) is the decrease in AUC when one feature's values are randomly shuffled. Larger decreases indicate more important variables. It is computed on the test set, so it describes which features the model relies on for new patients (funcml tutorial §10.3). The script reads the top predictor from the result instead of typing its name, so the next step keeps working if the ranking changes.

perm_cls <- interpret(fit_final, data_test, method = "permute",
                      metric = "auc", type = "prob", nsim = 50, seed = SEED)
plot(perm_cls)

perm_df <- as.data.frame(perm_cls$result$scores)
col_var <- intersect(c("feature", "Variable", "variable", "term"), names(perm_df))[1]
col_imp <- intersect(c("importance", "Importance", "mean_importance", "score"), names(perm_df))[1]
top_predictor <- perm_df %>% arrange(desc(.data[[col_imp]])) %>% slice_head(n = 1) %>% pull(.data[[col_var]])
cat("Top predictor:", top_predictor, "\n")
#> Top predictor: TOTAL13

Table 6: Top 10 predictors by permutation importance (mean decrease in AUC).

RankFeatureMean ΔAUCSD
1TOTAL13 (ADAS-Cog 13)0.0370.013
2CDRSB0.0140.010
3ST32TA0.0120.005
4ST29SV_norm0.0070.007
5Cer_d18_1_18_00.0050.003
6CR1_P179270.0050.004
7LDELTOTAL0.0040.004
8ST99TA0.0040.002
9VSNL1_P627600.0040.003
10TOTSCORE0.0030.004

Only TOTAL13 stands clearly apart. From rank 4 on, the standard deviations are as large as the means, so the order of these variables would change with another test set.

8.2 Effect of the top predictor: PDP and ALE

A partial dependence plot (PDP; Friedman 2001) averages the prediction over the data while the feature is set to each value; accumulated local effects (ALE; Apley and Zhu 2020) only compare predictions within narrow intervals of the feature, which avoids evaluating the model on impossible combinations when predictors are correlated, as cognitive scores are here.5

plot(interpret(fit_final, data_test, method = "pdp", features = top_predictor, type = "prob", pos_level = "Yes"))
plot(interpret(fit_final, data_test, method = "ale", features = top_predictor, type = "prob", pos_level = "Yes"))

Both plots show predicted risk rising with TOTAL13 (a higher ADAS-Cog score means more impairment). The rise is step-like, as expected from trees: the ALE has its steepest segments between about 12 and 15 and between about 20 and 23. The PDP plateaus above 30, where there are almost no patients, so the curve there is an extrapolation, not evidence.

8.3 Local explanation: SHAP

SHAP (Lundberg and Lee 2017) decomposes one prediction into additive feature contributions that sum to the difference between this prediction and the average prediction:

f(x) = E[f(z)] + Σi φi
top_patient  <- data_test[which.max(probs_test), , drop = FALSE]
shap_patient <- interpret(fit_final, data_test, method = "shap", newdata = top_patient,
                          type = "prob", nsim = 50, seed = SEED)
plot(shap_patient, kind = "waterfall")
Note: an illustrative case

This is the test patient with the highest predicted risk, an illustrative case rather than a typical patient. Notice that the two largest named contributions are MRI measures, not TOTAL13: global importance and one patient's explanation answer different questions.

Try it

Run interpret(fit_final, data_test, method = "ice", features = top_predictor, type = "prob", pos_level = "Yes") to see one curve per patient instead of the average, then explain the lowest-risk test patient with SHAP (which.min(probs_test)) and compare the two waterfalls (funcml tutorial §10.5 and §10.9).

9 Clinical Utility: Decision Curve Analysis

Decision curve analysis (Vickers and Elkin 2006) asks whether acting on the model is better than simple default strategies. At a threshold probability τ, the net benefit counts true positives and penalises false positives by the odds τ / (1 − τ), the weight a clinician implicitly gives to a false alarm when choosing τ:

NB(τ) = TP/n − (FP/n) · τ / (1 − τ)

The model is compared with "treat all" (everyone flagged) and "treat none" (net benefit 0). Script 05 reads both thresholds from the metrics file saved by script 02, so nothing is typed by hand.

df_eval <- data_test %>% mutate(proba_pred = predict(fit_final, data_test, type = "prob")[, "Yes"])
N <- nrow(df_eval); TP_all <- sum(df_eval$target == "Yes"); FP_all <- sum(df_eval$target == "No")
thresholds <- seq(0.01, 0.99, by = 0.01)
nb_model <- sapply(thresholds, function(pt) {
  pred <- df_eval$proba_pred >= pt
  (sum(pred & df_eval$target == "Yes") / N) - (sum(pred & df_eval$target == "No") / N) * (pt / (1 - pt))
})
nb_all <- (TP_all / N) - (FP_all / N) * (thresholds / (1 - thresholds))
#> Thresholds (validation set): low 0.124 | high 0.369

The model's net benefit is clearly above both reference strategies at low to moderate thresholds (up to about 0.5, which includes both operating points). It is small between 0.5 and 0.7 and close to zero, or slightly negative, around 0.7 to 0.75. At the lowest thresholds the model is close to "treat all", which is expected: if you are willing to accept many false alarms, flagging everyone costs little. The curve is irregular at high thresholds because only a few test patients have such high predictions.

10 Fairness Audit (05_dca_fairness.R)

For a metric m, the disparity across subgroups g is

Δm = maxg mg − ming mg, ΔAUC < 0.05 taken as no clinically meaningful disparity

The 0.05 bound is a pre-specified, project-specific target, not a validated standard (Rajkomar et al. 2018). Subgroups are sex, APOE-ε4 status (n_e4 >= 1) and education, split at the median of the test set, 16 years. A fixed 12-year cut-off was not used: almost all ADNI participants have at least 12 years of schooling (only 37 of 1,288 have fewer), which would leave a handful of patients in the low group. All metrics use the screening threshold τlow.

calculer_metriques <- function(truth, prob, seuil) {
  pred <- prob >= seuil
  tp <- sum(pred & truth == "Yes"); fp <- sum(pred & truth == "No")
  tn <- sum(!pred & truth == "No"); fn <- sum(!pred & truth == "Yes")
  data.frame(AUC = as.numeric(pROC::auc(truth, prob, levels = c("No", "Yes"), direction = "<")),
             Sensitivity = ifelse(tp + fn > 0, tp / (tp + fn), NA),
             Specificity = ifelse(tn + fp > 0, tn / (tn + fp), NA),
             PPV         = ifelse(tp + fp > 0, tp / (tp + fp), NA))
}
df_fairness <- df_eval %>% mutate(
  sexe        = ifelse(PTGENDER == "Homme", "Male", "Female"),
  apoe_risque = ifelse(n_e4 >= 1, "APOE-e4 Carrier", "Non-carrier"),
  education   = ifelse(PTEDUCAT >= median(PTEDUCAT, na.rm = TRUE), "High Education", "Low Education"))

audit <- function(var, label) df_fairness %>% group_by(Groupe = .data[[var]]) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), converters = sum(target == "Yes"),
            calculer_metriques(target, proba_pred, seuil_bas), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(Variable = label, .before = 1)
table_fairness <- bind_rows(audit("sexe", "Sex"), audit("apoe_risque", "APOE Status"), audit("education", "Education"))
table_fairness %>% group_by(Variable) %>% summarise(Delta_AUC = max(AUC) - min(AUC))
#> Education median (test set): 16 years
#> # A tibble: 6 × 8
#>   Variable    Groupe              n converters   AUC Sensitivity Specificity   PPV
#> 1 Sex         Female            118         27 0.888       0.963       0.714 0.5
#> 2 Sex         Male              140         26 0.848       0.808       0.658 0.35
#> 3 APOE Status APOE-e4 Carrier   127         35 0.824       0.914       0.5   0.410
#> 4 APOE Status Non-carrier       131         18 0.911       0.833       0.832 0.441
#> 5 Education   High Education    173         36 0.868       0.833       0.723 0.441
#> 6 Education   Low Education      85         17 0.883       1           0.603 0.386
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   Variable    Delta_AUC
#> 1 APOE Status    0.0868
#> 2 Education      0.0156
#> 3 Sex            0.0406

ΔAUC is 0.041 for sex, 0.087 for APOE-ε4 status (above the 0.05 bound) and 0.016 for education. APOE-ε4 carriers are detected with higher sensitivity (0.914 versus 0.833) but at the price of lower specificity (0.500 versus 0.832): more false positives in this subgroup. The sensitivity of 1.000 in the low-education group is 17 of 17 converters and is compatible with a wide range of true values. The subgroup counts add up to the totals of Section 7.3 (for example 26 + 21 = 47 converters detected among women and men), a useful check that no patient was lost.

Figure 9 and Table 7 show how the three risk levels distribute across subgroups. Carriers are classified High risk about three times as often as non-carriers (31.5% versus 10.7%), consistent with the higher baseline risk carried by the ε4 allele.

SubgroupLowModerateHigh

Try it

Replace seuil_bas by seuil_haut in audit() to audit the Rule-In threshold, and add a 95% interval to each subgroup AUC with pROC::ci.auc(target, proba_pred, levels = c("No", "Yes"), direction = "<"). Does the APOE disparity remain once the intervals are shown?

11 Temporal Robustness (03_temporal_robustness.R)

To check that the 24-month horizon is not arbitrary, a lighter version of the pipeline is repeated at 12, 24 and 36 months: three learners are benchmarked, XGBoost is fitted with default hyperparameters, permutation importance uses nsim = 10, and a fresh 80/20 split with seed 42 is drawn for each horizon. Its test AUC is therefore that of a different model from the tuned model of Section 5. The key step is the same as in Section 4: impute with the outcome columns excluded.

HORIZONS           <- c(12, 24, 36)
COMPARE_WITH_LEAKY <- FALSE

tester_horizon <- function(df, horizon_mois, leaky = FALSE) {
  df <- df %>% mutate(target = factor(if_else(event == 1 & time_to_event <= horizon_mois, "Yes", "No"),
                                      levels = c("No", "Yes")))
  keep   <- names(which(colMeans(is.na(df)) <= MAX_MISSING_PCT / 100))
  df_sel <- df %>%
    select(all_of(keep), -any_of(DROP_COLS)) %>%
    mutate(PTGENDER = factor(PTGENDER, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("Homme", "Femme")),
           n_e4 = str_count(GENOTYPE, "4"), GENOTYPE = factor(GENOTYPE))

  set.seed(SEED)                                              # split BEFORE imputation
  idx_test  <- sample(nrow(df_sel), size = round(TEST_FRACTION * nrow(df_sel)))
  train_raw <- df_sel[-idx_test, ];  test_raw <- df_sel[idx_test, ]

  if (!leaky) {
    vars_imp <- setdiff(names(train_raw), ID_COLS)
    rec <- recipe(~ ., data = train_raw[vars_imp]) %>%
      step_impute_knn(all_predictors(), neighbors = 5) %>% prep(training = train_raw[vars_imp])
    data_train <- bind_cols(train_raw[ID_COLS], bake(rec, new_data = train_raw[vars_imp]))
    data_test  <- bind_cols(test_raw[ID_COLS],  bake(rec, new_data = test_raw[vars_imp]))
  } else {                                                    # OLD, LEAKY: outcome columns in the recipe
    rec <- recipe(target ~ ., data = train_raw) %>% step_impute_knn(all_predictors()) %>% prep(training = train_raw)
    data_train <- bake(rec, new_data = NULL);  data_test <- bake(rec, new_data = test_raw)
  }

  vars_pred   <- setdiff(names(data_train), NON_PREDICTORS)
  formula_cls <- reformulate(vars_pred, response = "target")

  cmp <- compare_learners(data = data_train, formula = formula_cls,
                          models = c("glm", "ranger", "xgboost"),
                          resampling = cv(v = 5, seed = SEED), metrics = "auc", type = "prob", seed = SEED)
  cmp_list <- unclass(cmp)
  cmp_df   <- cmp_list[[which(sapply(cmp_list, function(x) is.data.frame(x) && "model" %in% names(x)))[1]]]

  fit_h <- fit(formula = formula_cls, data = data_train, model = "xgboost")
  probs <- predict(fit_h, data_test, type = "prob")[, "Yes"]
  pos <- probs[data_test$target == "Yes"]; neg <- probs[data_test$target == "No"]
  r <- rank(c(pos, neg))
  auc_test <- (sum(r[seq_along(pos)]) - length(pos) * (length(pos) + 1) / 2) / (length(pos) * length(neg))

  perm <- interpret(fit_h, data_test, formula = formula_cls, method = "permute",
                    metric = "auc", type = "prob", nsim = 10, seed = SEED)
  sc   <- perm$result$scores
  cv_  <- intersect(c("feature", "Variable", "variable", "term"), names(sc))[1]
  ci_  <- intersect(c("importance", "Importance", "mean_importance", "score"), names(sc))[1]
  top5 <- sc %>% arrange(desc(.data[[ci_]])) %>% slice_head(n = 5) %>% pull(.data[[cv_]])

  tibble(horizon = horizon_mois, imputation = if (leaky) "outcome in recipe (leaky)" else "predictors only",
         n_yes = sum(data_train$target == "Yes") + sum(data_test$target == "Yes"),
         n_no  = sum(data_train$target == "No")  + sum(data_test$target == "No"),
         auc_cv_xgboost = cmp_df %>% filter(model == "xgboost", metric == "auc") %>% pull(mean),
         auc_test = auc_test, top5_variables = paste(top5, collapse = ", "))
}
grid <- expand.grid(h = HORIZONS, leaky = if (COMPARE_WITH_LEAKY) c(TRUE, FALSE) else FALSE)
resultats_table <- map2(grid$h, grid$leaky, ~ tester_horizon(df_brut, .x, .y)) %>%
  bind_rows() %>% arrange(horizon, imputation)
print(resultats_table, width = Inf)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 7
#>   horizon imputation      n_yes  n_no auc_cv_xgboost auc_test top5_variables
#> 1      12 predictors only   124  1164          0.818    0.805 TOTAL13, CDRSB, ST29SV_norm, ABETA42, ST32TA
#> 2      24 predictors only   241  1047          0.816    0.866 TOTAL13, ST29SV_norm, Cer_d18_1_18_0, ST99TA, ST52TA
#> 3      36 predictors only   302   986          0.816    0.875 TOTAL13, Cer_d18_1_18_0, CDRSB, ST29SV_norm, Cer_d18_1_16_0

By default the script runs the corrected version only and writes outputs/temporal_robustness_table.csv. Setting COMPARE_WITH_LEAKY <- TRUE adds the earlier version, in which the outcome columns were inside the imputation recipe; that comparison gives the right-hand column of Table 8 and the dashed lines of Figure 10.

Table 8: Temporal robustness across prediction horizons (default XGBoost, 80/20 split, seed 42).

HorizonConvertersStableCV AUCTest AUCTest AUC with outcome in imputationTop 5 variables (corrected)
12 months1241,1640.8180.8050.807 (CV 0.852)TOTAL13, CDRSB, ST29SV_norm, ABETA42, ST32TA
24 months2411,0470.8160.8660.904 (CV 0.864)TOTAL13, ST29SV_norm, Cer_d18_1_18_0, ST99TA, ST52TA
36 months3029860.8160.8750.905 (CV 0.886)TOTAL13, Cer_d18_1_18_0, CDRSB, ST29SV_norm, Cer_d18_1_16_0

Letting event and time_to_event enter the imputation inflated the test AUC by 0.002 (12 months), 0.038 (24 months) and 0.030 (36 months), and the cross-validated AUC by 0.034 to 0.070, more on the training side because training rows were imputed with their own outcome. A leak of this kind is easy to introduce when a recipe is written as target ~ ., raises no error, and is not detected by a held-out split alone (Kaufman et al. 2012).

With the corrected imputation, the 24-month test AUC (0.866) is close to the tuned model of Section 5 (0.871), and test AUC is 0.805, 0.866 and 0.875 at 12, 24 and 36 months: comparable at 24 and 36 months and somewhat lower at 12 months, where only 124 patients convert. TOTAL13 is the first predictor at every horizon, but the rest of the ranking changes from one horizon to the next and from the tuned model. ABETA42 and MOCA (42% and 58% missing) were in the leaky top 5 at 24 and 36 months but not in the corrected ones, which is consistent with outcome-informed imputation having favoured heavily imputed variables, although the data do not prove it. The analysis supports "the signal does not depend on the exact horizon", not a precise ordering.

12 Prediction for a New Patient and Deployment

12.1 Three-level prediction

The function predire_nouveau_patient() of script 04 recodes the inputs, adds every column the recipe expects as NA, records which variables are measured and which are estimated, imputes with the saved recipe, predicts, and applies the three-level rule. It reads both thresholds from the saved metrics, so nothing is hard-coded:

fit_final        <- readRDS(proc_path(FILES$model))
metriques_modele <- readRDS(proc_path(FILES$metrics))
recipe_prep      <- readRDS(proc_path(FILES$recipe))
SEUIL_BAS  <- metriques_modele$seuil_bas
SEUIL_HAUT <- metriques_modele$seuil_haut

vars_attendues   <- metriques_modele$variables_modele
vars_recipe      <- recipe_prep$var_info %>% filter(role == "predictor") %>% pull(variable)
ref_recipe       <- recipe_prep$steps[[1]]$ref_data
niveaux_genotype <- levels(ref_recipe$GENOTYPE)
niveaux_ptgender <- levels(ref_recipe$PTGENDER)

predire_nouveau_patient <- function(patient_data, fit_final, recipe_prep, seuil_bas, seuil_haut) {
  p <- patient_data
  p$PTGENDER <- if ("PTGENDER" %in% names(p)) {
    if (is.numeric(p$PTGENDER)) factor(p$PTGENDER, levels = c(1, 2), labels = niveaux_ptgender)
    else factor(as.character(p$PTGENDER), levels = niveaux_ptgender)
  } else factor(NA, levels = niveaux_ptgender)
  p$GENOTYPE <- if ("GENOTYPE" %in% names(p)) factor(as.character(p$GENOTYPE), levels = niveaux_genotype)
                else factor(NA, levels = niveaux_genotype)
  p$n_e4 <- stringr::str_count(as.character(p$GENOTYPE), "4")

  for (col in setdiff(vars_recipe, names(p))) p[[col]] <- NA          # columns expected by the recipe

  presentes          <- intersect(vars_attendues, names(p))
  variables_mesurees <- presentes[!is.na(p[1, presentes])]
  variables_estimees <- presentes[ is.na(p[1, presentes])]

  p_imp <- bake(recipe_prep, new_data = p)
  miss  <- setdiff(vars_attendues, names(p_imp))
  if (length(miss) > 0) stop("Variables missing after bake(): ", paste(miss, collapse = ", "))
  p_imp <- p_imp %>% select(all_of(vars_attendues))

  proba <- predict(fit_final, p_imp, type = "prob")[, "Yes"]
  decision <- ifelse(proba >= seuil_haut, "Haut risque", ifelse(proba >= seuil_bas, "Risque modéré", "Risque faible"))
  list(probabilite_conversion = round(proba, 3), decision = decision,
       seuil_bas = seuil_bas, seuil_haut = seuil_haut,
       variables_mesurees = variables_mesurees, variables_estimees = variables_estimees)
}

nouveau_patient <- data.frame(RID = 9999, entry_age = 72, PTEDUCAT = 14, PTGENDER = 1,
  MMSCORE = 24, CDRSB = 4, CDGLOBAL = 0.5, MOCA = 22, FAQTRAVL = 3, TOTAL13 = 15,
  TOTSCORE = 20, LIMMTOTAL = 8, LDELTOTAL = 7, GENOTYPE = "3/4")
resultat <- predire_nouveau_patient(nouveau_patient, fit_final, recipe_prep, SEUIL_BAS, SEUIL_HAUT)
#> Low threshold (Youden): 0.124 | High threshold (Rule-In): 0.369
#> Probability: 25.3 % | Decision: Risque modéré
#> Measured variables: 13 of 53

In this example only 13 of the 53 predictors are measured; the other 40 (MRI, lipids, proteomics, CSF markers) are imputed from the five most similar training patients. The probability of 25.3% falls between the two thresholds, hence "Risque modéré" (the decision labels are in French because the app reuses them). Script 04 also saves data_train_reference.rds, the reference cohort the app uses to know which variables the model expects.

12.2 From model to application

The NeuroVigil application applies exactly this function behind a trilingual interface (French, English, Arabic). It loads the model, the recipe, the reference cohort and the metrics file saved by scripts 01 to 04, reads the two thresholds from the metrics file, and offers single-patient prediction, batch scoring from an Excel or CSV file, a prediction history and a PDF report. Because the thresholds, AUC and ECE are read from metriques_modele_2F.rds, retraining the model updates the application without changing its code. For each prediction it lists which variables were measured and which were estimated, the same distinction as variables_mesurees and variables_estimees above.

13 Discussion

The five-property approach is deliberately conjunctive: a model that fails one property is not ready for use, however well it does on the others. Here discrimination (test AUC 0.871) and clinical utility are good, calibration is acceptable, the explanations are consistent with clinical knowledge (cognitive scores and MRI measures dominate), and the fairness audit identifies one disparity worth acting on.

13.1 Limitations

Labels. A third of the "No" patients were followed for less than 24 months; part of the false positives may be future converters. Sample size. All test estimates rest on 258 patients and 53 converters, and the thresholds on 37 validation converters; the confidence intervals are wide and a single split was used. Model choice. XGBoost was chosen for interpretability tooling, not because it beat tuned ranger or gbm, which were not tuned. Calibration. Risk is under-estimated in the middle of the range, where the Moderate and High levels are separated. Fairness. APOE-ε4 carriers have a lower AUC and a specificity of only 0.500 at the screening threshold; subgroup intervals were not computed and the Rule-In threshold was not audited by subgroup. Deployment. New patients typically have many imputed predictors, a situation the test set does not represent. Generalisation. ADNI over-represents highly educated North American volunteers, and there is no external validation.

13.2 Next steps

Model time to conversion directly with a survival learner, so that censored patients contribute correctly. Replace the single split by repeated or nested cross-validation, and tune ranger and gbm under the same protocol before choosing a learner. Recalibrate the probabilities on the validation set and check the effect on the Moderate/High boundary. Report subgroup confidence intervals, audit the Rule-In threshold by subgroup, and study whether APOE-specific thresholds reduce the disparity. Measure how performance degrades as fewer variables are measured, to tell users when a prediction is too uncertain. Finally, validate the model on an independent, more diverse cohort (for example NACC, or Moroccan clinical data) before any clinical claim.

14 Conclusion

NeuroVigil shows the full funcml workflow on a real clinical problem: cv() to fix the resampling, compare_learners() and tune() to choose and set a learner, fit() for the final model, and interpret() for importance, effects, individual explanations and calibration. Around these calls, the project adds the steps a clinical model needs: a split and an imputation that cannot leak the outcome, thresholds chosen on separate data, decision curves, a subgroup audit and a robustness check. The most useful lesson for students is probably the leak of Section 11: a single target ~ . in a recipe inflated the test AUC by up to 0.038 without any error message. The model reaches a test AUC of 0.871 with acceptable calibration, and its next test is an independent cohort outside ADNI.

Software

The analysis uses R with funcml (modelling, tuning, interpretation), recipes (KNN imputation), the tidyverse (Wickham et al. 2019), xgboost (Chen and Guestrin 2016), ranger, gbm and pROC (Robin et al. 2011). The application uses shiny, DT, readxl, writexl and base64enc. Script 02 writes the exact R and package versions of the run to outputs/sessionInfo_02.txt.

Code: github.com/AyaLahlifi/NeuroVigil. Application: neuropredictai.shinyapps.io/NeuroVigil_App. funcml: github.com/ielbadisy/funcml and its tutorial.

Footnotes

  1. Do not restore a saved workspace: NeuroVigil.Rproj disables it on purpose. An object left in the global environment can mask a function; for example, an object called ece masks the funcml function of the same name. Restart R (Ctrl+Shift+F10 in RStudio) before source("scripts/run_all.R"). ↩
  2. Two common remedies are to exclude patients followed for less than the horizon, which loses data and can bias the sample towards longer-followed patients, or to model time to conversion with a survival method, which uses the censored follow-up correctly (Section 13.2). ↩
  3. With 53 converters and 205 non-converters there are 53 × 205 = 10,865 pairs; an AUC of 0.871 means the converter is ranked higher in 87.1% of them (ties count half). The DeLong interval (DeLong, DeLong, and Clarke-Pearson 1988) is based on the same pairwise view. ↩
  4. funcml's calibration header (ECE = 0.0541) and the manual computation (0.056) use different bins, so the two numbers differ slightly. The difference is far smaller than the uncertainty of either estimate with 258 patients; we report the manual value because its binning is shown in the code. ↩
  5. A PDP for TOTAL13 averages predictions in which a patient's TOTAL13 is set to, say, 35 while their MMSE and CDR-SB stay normal, a combination that does not occur. ALE avoids this by only using patients whose TOTAL13 is already close to each value. The funcml tutorial (§10.4 and §10.6) gives the formulas. ↩
